entry.title: SAP Ariba, SAP Fieldglass and SAP S/4HANA ERP solutions for public healthcare
entry.content:
Author: Allan Soo

Introduction

Healthcare public sector procurement spend is among the largest across the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). In 2021, 31.9% of all public procurement spend touches on public healthcare and infrastructure [1]. Nearly 75% of public spend on healthcare came from taxpayers [2]. With an ageing population and a shrinking taxpayer base, governments across the world are grappling with these fiscal challenges. One solution is to deploy effective spend management, procurement solutions across cost-intensive sectors of the economy to keep costs down.

Figure depicting the percentage government expenditure across the OECD-EU countries for 2023 [3]. Public sector procurement across the OECD-EU markets was 14.7% (2023), an increase of 0.9% compared to 2019.  

Why an effective, public procurement platform is crucial for public healthcare and governments?

Public procurement in healthcare is one of the most regulated forms of purchasing dealing with hospitals, pharmacies, and qualified suppliers. This requires complex compliance to purchasing pharmaceutical ingredients, chemicals and other regulated products to be compliant to public healthcare agencies. An example is the procurement of surgical implants and tools which must comply with the Therapeutic Goods Association (TGA) and other dangerous goods regulations.

Healthcare public procurement is becoming a significant challenge for governments worldwide due to factors such as an ageing population, rising deficits and total debts, the high costs of running healthcare facilities, and increased health and safety regulations.

Track spend and compliance across cost-intensive healthcare segments by different categories with SAP Ariba Category Management, SAP Ariba Intake Management and SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle Performance Management

SAP Ariba Category Management gives public sector healthcare purchasers the tools to track spend goals on their most cost-intensive areas of their agency including high-tech equipment, specialized hospital beds, pharmaceutical purchases and more.

The solution gives public healthcare purchasers the option to manage supplier performance and track these against budgets, manage funds and investments assigned and set to them by the government.

The solution also offers customers a 360-degree visibility into the supplier’s healthcare certifications and qualifications, making sure that they comply to directives and maximize compliance across all purchases made for the public facilities. For example, Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) license for Australia, Wholesale Distribution Authorisation for EU suppliers supplying medicinal products, and Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency certification for medicinal product manufacturing in the United Kingdom.

Adverse events can then be monitored using SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance Management to manage supplier risks appropriately. 3rd party data such as D&B can give government buyers additional intelligence on the market risk of that supplier such as sustainability, supply chain exposure, and aid in calculating inherent and residual risk scoring…and so on. Up to 25 custom risk scores can be applied to the healthcare supplier in SAP Ariba Supplier Risk.

Renegotiate and manage multiple quotes across healthcare suppliers to drive cost savings with finance

To keep costs down, buyers have the ability with SAP Ariba Sourcing and Procurement for Public Sector in SAP S/4HANA, to manage different quotes and renegotiate prices with existing suppliers to obtain better deals. For example, evaluating the procurement of multiple MRI and X-ray machines, and different existing drug prices to encourage better competition between pharmaceutical suppliers to drive down prices.

Buyers can take advantage of the SAP Taulia Private Cloud solution with SAP S/4HANA and Dynamic Discounting feature where fast, early account payable transactions towards suppliers can lead to discounted cash savings that yield improved bottom line benefits for public healthcare finance customers.

Connect SAP Ariba Sourcing and SAP Ariba Buying solutions to the SAP S/4HANA ERP for high-level spend management and monitoring

Go beyond purchasing and ordering with high-level dashboard spend visibility [4] to track the list of purchase orders with SAP Ariba Central Procurement with SAP Ariba Buying (3EN) and SAP Ariba Buying, with guided buying capabilities (2NV) into SAP S/4HANA. Easily track the process flow of your purchases and export accounting documents to SAP finance and accounting solutions. Use three-way matching against invoice, purchase order and goods receipt to ensure that cost information is accurate. Request quotes from suppliers, allocate budget and discuss on pricing terms.

One highly relevant area for this is the operational procurement of medical apparel, protective equipment, gloves and face masks. You as the buyer want the tools to negotiate with suppliers on favorable pricing terms, sort price lists in Catalogs available over the SAP Business Network, and see the list of purchase orders, invoices and goods receipts in one place. You can set estimated budgets throughout the quotation process and track how far below under the target price you are able to get the costs down to attain cost savings.

Figure showing SAP Ariba Buying and Invoicing solution where healthcare purchasers can track how far below taxpayer funded budget they can obtain when purchasing medical supplies like gloves.

With these solutions, healthcare public sector buyers and public finance can move away from matching for accuracies and scrutinize cost details on these items and work collaboratively with other departments to find alternative suppliers and products that offer cheaper and better-quality substitutes.  

Leverage AI solutions for contracts management

SAP Ariba Contract Intelligence by Icertis SolEx has contract authoring capabilities that are bolstered by AI to automate much of the clause generation that is in line with the public healthcare industry and to drive compliance. Examples can include authoring in sustainability criteria, medical manufacturing license requirements from suppliers, and assigning responsibilities on direct suppliers and their affiliates. By automating the contract lifecycle, lead times can be reduced and anomalies within contract clauses can be detected and flagged for risk mitigation. The solution helps users identify contract leakage risks to prevent cost blowouts and put boundaries on spend conditions for public healthcare purchases. Risk scores on suppliers can be imported from SAP Ariba Supplier Risk to SAP Ariba Contracts to guide contract awarding decisions so that risk-aware awarding decisions can be made. Managing suppliers is part of the public sector procurement responsibility to ensure that government healthcare agencies continue receiving the best outcomes for the budget they are given with the right contracts in place.

Put cost guardrails on healthcare goods and services procured

With WK value contracts [5] in SAP S/4HANA, SAP Ariba Contracts [6] users can set guardrails against overspending on suppliers. Given that in healthcare settings the quantity of goods can be non-negotiable, SAP Ariba Contracts offers the flexibility to adjust quantity (through quantity contracts) and assign other attributes such as discounts on purchased goods through supplier collaboration and negotiations. Buyers can set cost parameters on the value contracts and publish it through the Cloud Integration Gateway to SAP S/4HANA. Purchase cost data can then be ingested by finance solutions to monitor and act on the financial performance of the health agency.

Smart Peppol invoicing with SAP S/4HANA and SAP Ariba Central Invoice Management

With eInvoicing solutions offered with SAP Documents and Reporting Compliance (cloud edition) within S/4HANA ERP Public Cloud Edition, SAP Business Network via SAP Integration Suite, and SAP Ariba Central Invoice Management - Peppol compliant documents can be exchanged to help government healthcare sectors align with eInvoicing compliance requirements or eliminate the use of physical paper. Eliminating physical paperwork and complying to Peppol eInvoicing means enhancing fraud-prevention systems in place to build trust with the public and install financial protections, improves productivity and minimizes errors in costing amounts.  Peppol is used by over 40 countries worldwide for business-to-government transactions, and is becoming a standardized, secure method of receiving invoices from the private sector supplier base by government agencies. Public hospitals and other healthcare agencies can examine and analyze invoice costs based on the high-fidelity information supplied electronically within the system, making it easily auditable for finance.

AI-driven Statement of Work (SOW) creations in SAP Fieldglass to alleviate workloads and focus on the things that matter

Minimize admin work and hire contractors to help comply to a variety of laws during the SOW creation process. Use the GenAI solution at SAP to identify opportunities to control costs during the SOW creation and reduce document creation times by about 71% by inputting titles, summaries and extracting data from PDF documents. With freed-up workloads, users can focus on the quality, risk and service traits of the contract (such as proper skills matching for best labour productivity outcomes). An example includes SOW creation for biohazardous health waste disposal services and scoping the boundaries of work, and clearly stating what services are in and out of scope and using SOW teams feature to collaborate with non-procurement colleagues on budget planning with finance that addresses high-spend service categories.

Improved SOW rates negotiation and cost management features on contracted services

Service buyers can negotiate for better rates post-agreement, automate offboarding signatures to cease spend, ensure hours worked are fulfilled by the contractors, reallocation of unspent SOW funds back to master SOW, inactivate cost centers when they are no longer used, and trigger alerts when rates vary away from agreed ones. These are features that are offered by SAP Fieldglass to service buyers in public healthcare settings to put a lid on costs.

Picture this, you need to onboard technicians to provide maintenance and calibration services for the complex equipment that the hospital has. Your rates need to be specified clearly, and any pay deviations need to be notified to the service buyer, clear start-end dates for the services and so on need to be in the SOW for legal reasons. You use the GenAI feature to produce an SOW quickly, double check the contents of this document, and have the work order issued. Skills are clearly specified for the job to minimize lead times onsite, and the best labour-hire is made. Therefore, costs are controlled, and the best productivity is obtained for maintenance work at the hospital.

Support green procurement practices

SAP Ariba Sourcing integrates with the suite of SAP S/4HANA Cloud ERP sustainability solutions to drive green procurement practices across the public healthcare sector. Given that Scope 3 contributes to around 79% of total carbon emissions [7] for this sector across the OECD markets, governments can use SAP tools to drive sustainable procurement practices on their direct suppliers. Examples including procuring gloves with a low product carbon footprint, high recycled content, and rubber data to ensure that illegal deforestation has not contributed to its production.

Alongside SAP Ariba Supplier Management, SAP Fieldglass and SAP Ariba Contracts, public healthcare sectors can manage risk appropriately and enforce sustainability practices and compliance on suppliers and contractors. This includes due diligence screening solutions on a supplier’s human rights and deforestation records, having the right sustainability credentials, and embedding sustainability due diligence into the core operational and strategic sourcing processes from procurement to the ERP environment. Given the mandates that governments must meet for their own net-zero, human rights and material circularity directives - SAP Ariba, SAP Fieldglass and SAP ERP Sustainability solutions provide a comprehensive suite of products to drive decarbonization and compliance in the public healthcare space. Partner solutions on the SAP app store can be used to enrich supplier data with sustainability scores and other external intel.

Tap into the SAP Spend Intelligence in SAP Business Data Cloud solution for rich data reporting on procurement spend

Enrich healthcare spend data with other SAP Business Data Cloud products to gain deeper insights into the entire healthcare organization’s finance and spend data. SAP Spend Intelligence offers customers a large variety of data products it can ingest. For example, sustainability, risk, contract leakages and off-contract purchase order spend.  By providing strategic and operational insights into a public healthcare’s spend, buyers can optimize for and eliminate out non-compliance and uses AI and machine learning to automatically allocate spend categories neatly for interpretation. SAP Joule can be employed to clean and present cluttered data in a meaningful way that helps drive high-level decision-making processes which maximizes healthcare spend impacts and cuts down maverick and unwanted tail spend.

Conclusion

SAP Ariba, SAP Fieldglass and SAP S/4HANA ERP solutions provide finance and spend management solutions that offer customers the tools to keep up to date with the latest innovations in driving cost savings, optimize spend, manage down risks, reduce fraud and work collaboratively with public sector finance teams in government. Given the significance of public healthcare sectors across developed markets, innovative procurement spend management solutions play a key role in controlling costs in a high-expenditure industry. For years to come, healthcare expenses are projected to increase with an ageing population, rising deficits and living cost challenges.

This requires a comprehensive, suite of solutions for the public sector that leverages best-of-breed AI and solution offerings that advance the modernization of public sector procurement and finance operations. Governments have a responsibility to foster trust, comply to own directives, address fiscal challenges across the economy for the wellbeing of citizens, and deliver services cost-effectively to the public.

entry.title: Adoption Isn’t a Phase, It’s a Relationship
entry.content:
If you know me, you know I love an analogy. It’s always helpful to make new information make sense by likening it to something we already understand.

In my role here at SAP, I talk about adoption a lot. It’s a point that I (and my wonderful team, Solution Value Advisory) really push with our customers, who sometimes think of adoption as a step in the overall process, something you do after go-live.  So, my analogy for today is to look at adoption like a relationship, because it’s never just about the software, but about the people and how they interact with the system and each other.

It’s not much of a stretch, really. At the start, it’s a mix of excitement, a little confusion, and commitment that comes with bringing something new into your life, and hoping it thrives, grows, and has the support of people around you.


The honeymoon stage
 In my last role several years back, I worked on Ariba solution implementations. Being on a shared services team, I got to stick my hands into a lot of different customers’ Ariba deployments. It felt great, for the customer and for me, to reach what felt like a finish line: go-live. That point of the new solution(s) going live after months of setup and testing. The vibes were always good - everyone was hopeful, users explored the system, performed tests. Teams got trained. There was that spark of possibility, that sense of this time, things will be different.

But just like any new relationship, the shine fades if the day-to-day connection isn’t nurtured. Old habits creep back in, shortcuts resurface. And, before long, that beautiful new tool starts gathering dust.  Remember, adoption doesn’t end at go-live, that’s when it begins.


Relationships thrive on consistency, and so do systems
Healthy adoption looks a lot like a healthy partnership: steady, intentional, and full of small moments that build trust.

It’s when someone logs in and sees that their preferences were remembered. It’s when data syncs across systems, so people stop fighting with spreadsheets and endless back-and-forth email. It’s when users realize the tool makes their jobs easier, not harder. It keeps the relationship alive.

But breakdowns don’t usually happen with a bang, but a fizzle. Users don’t revolt, they quietly disengage. They skip the process “just this once.” Then they stop trusting the data, because the process is getting skipped and they can’t find what they were looking for. And now something that was originally set up to create efficiency is now only causing frustration, and becomes a pain in the…well, you know. 😊

In my work with customers, I see this all the time.  I work a lot with customers on their supplier management processes especially, and I see a lot of this disengagement when it comes to onboarding. Tools like SAP Cloud Identity Services and SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle & Performance (SLP) can be super powerful, but they depend on trusted data and consistency. If people don’t understand why something matters, they won’t invest in making it work.

The love language of AI is good data
Now we’re entering a new chapter, one where AI tools like SAP Joule are ready to help make our jobs easier. But even Joule, which might seem like magic when you see it presented, needs a foundation of trust. This has been my main message of the year - reminding people that AI doesn’t make magic out of thin air, rather it builds on what we give it. If data is messy, disconnected, or if established processes are underused, Joule’s insights will be, too.

(Pausing here for a shoutout to anyone who was at the Customer Success Day in NYC earlier this year where I did a whole session to essentially say, “Garbage in, garbage out”. The highlight, at least to me, was my AI-generated Ariba song parody of Naughty by Nature’s O.P.P.  Who’s down with SLP? Yeah you know me!)

But back to my relationship analogy, think of it this way: if you never talk to your partner, you can’t expect them to finish your sentences. Joule works the same way. The relationship only deepens when we communicate through connected, clean, and well-adopted systems. 


Adoption is ongoing care.
As I said before, adoption isn’t a task. We don’t “complete” adoption. We maintain it. We check in with our users, we update them on changes, and we listen when something isn’t working and adjust before resentment sets in.  The most successful customers I see are those who treat adoption as a living process. Not just implementing technology, but inviting it into their company culture. When adoption is healthy, everything else (innovation, automation, AI, etc.) starts to flow naturally.  But just like any great relationship, it takes attention, empathy, and patience.


I encourage you all to stay in tune with our roadmap, as there’s a lot of exciting stuff to come in 2026 when it comes to AI in SAP. But as you read up on that and start to think how cool it will be and how much time it will save to have all of those new capabilities, remember that now is the time to build the foundation for that new relationship. 

If you have any doubts about how well your company is adopting your solutions and how you’re doing on usage in comparison to other customers, do reach out to your CSM who can either help, or can pull in the right people to have that conversation. Sometimes that person is me, so say hi and maybe I'll share my library of Ariba song parodies.

entry.title: SAP Ariba Roadmap: Quality Gates Checklist in SAP Cloud ALM
entry.content:
Imagine you’re halfway through your Ariba implementation, and suddenly you discover that key testing activities from earlier phases weren’t completed. What a roadblock! You start to get anxious and stressed and you are wondering how to solve this problem and still meet the deadlines. If you’ve been involved in a project before, you know that sinking feeling all too well.

This is exactly where Quality Gates come to the rescue. At the end of each phase - Prepare, Explore, Realize, and Deploy - there is a task specifically designed to help you check whether all the key deliverables have been completed, align with stakeholders, validate the activities and configurations executed, and think of mitigation plans if something was missed. Think of it as your project’s safety net, catching issues before they grow into bigger problems.

For those using Road Map Viewer, you will have a ‘Conduct Project Quality Gate’ task and an Excel file as an accelerator with easy questions and answers to help you validate your deliveries. You will have to download it and share it with other stakeholders when needed.

But here’s the big news: if you’re working in SAP Cloud ALM, the Quality Gate Checklist is now available directly within the system. That means you no longer need to download the Excel file. You can answer questions, track the status of each item, add comments, and tag the responsible stakeholders - all in one place. This makes Quality Gates more actionable and ensures everyone on the project team stays aligned. See the video below with an example of how to locate this information and answer the questions.

 

With this improvement, your SAP Ariba projects can start 2026 on the right foot. Quality Gates Checklist in SAP Cloud ALM makes it easier than ever to reduce risks, stay aligned, and keep your project moving smoothly.

Feel free to share your comments, suggestions, or feedback in this blog post or directly in Road Map Viewer. We will be happy to assist and improve the quality of our roadmaps!

entry.title: SAP Ariba Supplier Management & Risk 2602 Release Key Innovations Preview
entry.content:
Supplier Lifecycle & Performance

Ability to Restrict Hierarchy Level Selection for Department and Region in Questionnaire Configuration (SLP-2309)

With this feature, template creators can now configure hierarchy level selection restrictions for Department and Region question types in the same way they can for Commodity questions. Respondents can select only within specified hierarchy levels, improving accuracy in data selection and reducing manual review and correction efforts. (Learn more.)


Integration Support for Supplier Qualification Status (SLP-2387)

This feature adds support for synchronizing supplier qualification status to integrated ERP systems using custom generic fields. This change allows you to access up-to-date qualification information directly in the ERP system, facilitating automated decision-making processes such as blocking suppliers with expired qualifications. (Learn more.)


Ability to Restrict the Number of Commodity, Region, and Department Answers in Process Intake Forms (SLP-2392)

This feature enables you to configure the maximum number of answers process initiators can add to Commodity, Region, and Department questions in process intake forms. (Learn more.)


Ability to Perform Real-time Validation and Version Comparison for Supplier Questionnaire (SLP-2377)

This feature enables you to validate the data in real-time for supplier responses to external questionnaires. It allows buyers to compare validated current responses with previously approved versions. This enhances data accuracy and compliance with buyer standards. It also accelerates supplier onboarding. (Learn more.)


Additional Project Header Fields for Conditional Approvals (SLP-2386)

This feature increases the number of project header fields available for creating conditional approval workflows beyond the current six fields. This change allows you to create more conditional approval flows per questionnaire. (Learn more.)


Ability to Restrict Hierarchy Level Selection for Department and Region in Modular Questionnaire Configuration (SLP-2408)

With this feature, template creators can configure hierarchy level selection restrictions in the modular questionnaire template for Department and Region question types in the same way they can for Commodity questions . Respondents can select only within specified hierarchy levels, improving accuracy in data selection and reducing manual review and correction efforts. (Learn more.)


Additional AI Copilot Joule Capabilities for Finding Suppliers, Supplier Contacts, and Supplier Management Projects (SLP-2411)

This feature adds capabilities for using AI copilot Joule to find more information about suppliers and supplier management projects, including approval status and pending approvers for projects created by the current user, qualified and preferred suppliers, and suppliers with expiring or expired certificates. It also enhances the scenario for finding supplier contact information. (Learn more.)

 

Supplier Performance Evaluations in SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance (NGSM-2269)

This feature allows buyers to create and manage programs for conducting periodic supplier performance evaluations, which evaluate suppliers for performance based on key indicators determined by your organization. (Learn more.)

 

Supplier Risk

Ability to Enhance Risk Control Effectiveness by Automating Residual Risk Calculation (NGSM-1273)

This feature enables you to automate the effectiveness review of risk controls by using modular questionnaire scoring based on predefined criteria, eliminating the need for manual assessment. (Learn more.)


Ability to Create an Engagement Request from a Supplier Request Data (SRISK-1878)

This feature enables you to create engagement requests directly from approved supplier requests, removing repetitive manual steps and ensuring data consistency between supplier requests and engagement requests. You will receive a pop up message once the engagement request is created. (Learn more.)


Enhancing Supplier Risk Exposure API By Adding New Data Fields in Response (SRISK-1887)

This feature introduces a new version of the Supplier Risk Exposure API. In addition with the exposure details in the response, this new version has additional two fields data in the API response. (Learn more.)

entry.title: Balancing Conflicting Priorities of Procurement and Supply Chain
entry.content:
From Factory Floor to Forecast: What Matt Donegan’s Procurement Stories Reveal About Where SAP Customers Are Heading 🚀

If you’ve ever wondered why procurement debates can get so heated—especially in manufacturing—Matt Donegan’s podcast conversation is a masterclass in the real-world tension behind “simple” sourcing decisions. 🧩 Beneath the lighthearted dog-and-TikTok opener, Matt digs into an issue SAP customers and partners know well: direct materials procurement isn’t just about savings—it’s about keeping production running, protecting quality, and managing risk across a supply chain that’s often far less predictable than it looks on a dashboard. ⚙️

What makes Matt’s perspective especially valuable is that it’s grounded in plant-site reality. He’s lived the pressure of missing ingredients, uncertain shipments, and the ripple effect that one supplier decision can create across operations. And for organizations modernizing with SAP, his stories point to a clear message: the future belongs to teams that connect sourcing strategy with shop-floor execution—using data, collaboration, and technology that people actually adopt. 📈

Direct vs. Indirect: Why the “Lifeblood” Spend Gets Different Rules 🧠

One of the most important framing points in the discussion is the distinction between direct materials, indirect materials, and services—because the business consequences are radically different. 🏭

  • Direct materials are inputs that become part of the finished product. They’re planned against forecasts, tied to production schedules, and directly impact what customers receive on a daily basis. ✅
  • Indirect materials support the business (think facility supplies, office goods, and warehouse items), but don’t appear on the bill of materials. 🧻
  • Services keep operations running—from maintenance to repairs to cleaning and MRO-related work. 🛠️

Why does this matter to SAP customers and partners? Because direct procurement runs on a different clock and carries different risk. A late shipment of a key ingredient can halt a production line—turning a “good deal” into an expensive disruption. ⏱️

Plant Managers Aren’t Graded on Savings—They’re Graded on Output 🎯

Matt’s biggest insight is also one of the most practical: plant leaders are running a business inside the business. 📦 They manage inputs, transform them, and ship outputs—and their priority is being a reliable supplier to their customers.

From that lens, “success” looks like:

  • First-pass quality (materials meet spec without rework) ✅
  • On-time, in-full delivery (OTIF) (materials arrive when and how much is needed) 📅
  • Available-to-promise reliability (customers can trust commitments) 🤝

This is where procurement gets tricky: centralized sourcing teams may be measured primarily on year-over-year savings, while operations teams are measured on uptime and performance. 📊 The result is a familiar tug-of-war: cost optimization versus production certainty.

For SAP ecosystems, this is a reminder that transformation isn’t just system change—it’s KPI alignment and governance design. 🧭

The Real Pain Point: Global Supply Chains Still Have “Visibility Gaps” 🌍

One of Matt’s most vivid stories is about overseas procurement: sending a PO, getting a quick confirmation, and then enduring weeks of uncertainty. 🚢

Even when suppliers are reliable, international logistics introduces unpredictable variables:

  • port delays
  • customs holds
  • limited tracking precision
  • last-mile scheduling issues
  • constraints on receiving capacity at the plant 🧱

Matt highlights a dimension many teams underestimate: the human and physical reality of receiving. Materials don’t just “arrive.” Someone must unload, inspect, store safely (sometimes in specialized containers), and route it into production. 👷

For SAP customers, this underscores why visibility isn’t just a “nice-to-have.” It is operational resilience. And for partners, it reinforces the value of designs that connect procurement, logistics, inventory, and quality processes into one continuous picture. 🧩

Consignment: The Underused Strategy That Solves Two Problems at Once 💡

One of the most actionable tactics discussed is consignment inventory, which Matt calls a best friend—and for good reason. 🤝

In a consignment model:

  • the supplier ships material to the buyer’s site
  • the buyer does not pay until the material is pulled for use
  • inventory can sit nearby as a buffer without burdening working capital 💰

This creates two strategic advantages:

  1. Operational safety: the plant has backup stock when overseas shipments slip. 🛡️
  2. Working capital relief: millions in inventory can be available without sitting on the buyer’s balance sheet. 📉

The catch? Consignment depends on strong supplier trust—typically built through years of partnership and reliable consumption patterns. 🧱 This is an important point for procurement leaders: resilience often comes from relationship maturity, not just contract terms.

The Collaboration Playbook: Data, Shared Strategy, and Stakeholder Buy-In 📊

When asked how organizations can reduce friction between central sourcing and operations, Matt returns to a simple idea: be data-driven—and bring stakeholders along early. 🧾

He describes an internal “negotiation” process between sourcing and plant teams:

  • which suppliers are non-negotiable due to quality risk
  • where contracts can be rebalanced without harming performance
  • how allocation (local vs. overseas) can hedge risk over time ⚖️

The critical enablers here are:

  • shared metrics (not just siloed KPIs) 📐
  • supplier performance data (quality, OTIF, rework rates) 🔍
  • tools people actually use (adoption matters as much as capability) ✅

For SAP customers, this is a blueprint: procurement transformation succeeds when the system supports cross-functional decision-making—not when it simply digitizes old silos. 🏗️

Future-Facing Take: AI Will Elevate the Human Side of Procurement 🤖➡️🧑‍🤝‍🧑

entry.title: Troubleshooting Ariba-Joule Integration errors
entry.content:
Introduction:🚀 Cracking the SAP Ariba–Joule Integration common errors:

Over the past few months, I’ve seen a common pattern across multiple customer implementations: brilliant landscapes struggling with Navigation Flow glitches, incomplete Transactional prompts, or inconsistent User Sync—all caused by a handful of tiny but critical configuration gaps across Ariba, IAS, IPS, and Build Work Zone.

To help accelerate troubleshooting and avoid post‑go‑live surprises, I’ve put together a practical breakdown of the most recurring issues and the exact fixes that have consistently stabilized the integration.

If you're enabling Joule for Ariba or supporting customers on their journey, this article will save you hours of guesswork. 🔧💡

Common issues with Navigation flow and resolution: 

Scenario 1:Navigational prompts intermittently return data

Sample prompts: Go my approvals, my task, create engagement request, created sourcing project, open supplier profile etc   

Cause: This could happen, if user has been assigned more than 150 groups in Ariba and those groups are being replicated to IAS and then to Build work zone.  To verify if the issue is due to roles replicated to BWZ,  login to BWZ and user will get error “HTTP ERROR 431”. 

Resolution: Replicate only those standard groups to BWZ which are required for Ariba-Joule integration. You can achieve this by adding a filter parameter ariba.applications.group.filter in the IPS source system (the source system configured to fetch users and groups from Ariba https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/joule-integration-with-sap-ariba-setup-guide/ba-p/14240003 ). Using this filter ensures that only the required groups—and users assigned to those groups—are synchronized from Ariba to IAS and subsequently to BWZ.

Sample value: (displayName eq "Sourcing Agent" or displayName eq "Sourcing Approver")

Important Notes

  • Navigational flow works only with standard groups.
  • If customers assign only custom roles to users in Ariba, they must still replicate the required standard groups from Ariba → IAS → BWZ.
  • Custom groups are not supported, SAP is considering for future release 
  • This filtering process does not impact customer‑specific role assignments:
    • Customers may continue using their custom groups assignment in Ariba as usual
    • Since custom groups map back to standard roles, any Joule‑relevant standard roles tied to custom roles will still function properly through this filtered sync.
  • Recommendation:
    • Maintain a list of standard groups required for Joule navigation.
    • Additionally replicate customer‑specific custom groups only to ensure that all Ariba users sync correctly to CIS

Steps to maintain the parameter:

  • Login to CIS and navigate to identity provision
  • Source system à look for the source system which is created to fetch the user/groups from Ariba
  • Edit and maintain the parameter and run the IPS job as described previously
List of standard roles which are required for Ariba joule Navigational scenario:

Supplier Registration Manager

Supplier Manager

Supplier Qualification Manager

Supplier Risk ESG User

Purchasing Administrator

Supplier Risk Engagement Requestor

Financial Processing Analyst

Supplier Risk Evaluation Expert

AuditBuyer

Supplier Risk Provider Registration Expert

Purchasing Agent

Joule Supplier Profile User

Invoice Manager

Sourcing Project Administrator

Purchasing Manager

Sourcing Agent

Report Manager

Limited Event Administrator

Receiving Manager

Junior Sourcing Agent

Manual Order Processor

SM Questionnaire Manager

Tax Manager

Supplier Risk Engagement Governance Analyst

Purchasing User

Supplier Qualification Request Manager

Executive Approver

Supplier Risk User

Sourcing Approver

Supplier Risk Report Expert

Category Buyer

Supplier Risk Engagement Expert

Supplier Risk Engagement Analyst

Sourcing Manager

Operational Junior Sourcing Agent

Supplier Risk Manager

Supplier Risk Configuration Expert

Supplier Request Manager

SM Process Manager

Event Administrator

Scenario 2:  Error “The application cannot be opened”

Resolution: Create a destination under the sub-account which has been created for joule. Make sure destination name is “NavigationService” follow the below article for more details.

https://help.sap.com/docs/joule/integrating-joule-with-sap/configure-destination-to-use-navigation-service?locale=en-US&q=+NavigationService

Steps:

  • Login to Joule Sub-account
  • Click connectivity à Destination
  • Click create

Scenario 3: Error: You need different permissions to perform this action or I am having trouble processing your request.

Cause : This happen when user doesn’t have the required access in Ariba or if they have the required access, joule related standard roles are not assigned to user in BWZ after replication.  

To verify the roles in BWZ, login to BWZ

  • Check User Role Assignments: In the settings à Identity Provisioning
  • Within "Explore Role Assignments",enter the user ID experiencing the issue
  • Review the list of roles and permissions assigned to the user

Resolution: As described in scenario 1 navigation flow, maintain the joule roles in source system parameter run the job. This will synchronize the user and groups between ariba , IAS and BWZ. Make sure roles are assigned to users in ariba as well. Login to BWZ and verify the roles once again:

Common issues with Transactional flow and resolution:

Scenario 1:When user enters any transactional prompt in joule, user gets results as an informational data.

Sample prompts: List of recent purchases

Cause: This happens when ibn_target not found at the backend. In simple words, the formation synchronization did not happen between the include system despite the fact status of the formation is ready.  

Resolution: Login to global account, exclude and include Ariba buyer and sourcing system within the formations.

 

Scenario 2: When user enters a transactional prompt, there is no response

Cause: This happens when there is no dependencies added to the das-ias applications in CIS

Resolution:

  • Login to IAS
  • Navigate to applications and search for “das-ias” and look for the entry which is there for the sub-account which is created for joule
  • Navigate to dependency section, make sure to maintain APIs for Procurement and Sourcing applications

Delayed User synchronization between Ariba and Cloud identify service: IPS Jobs are getting stuck in running status for few hours  

Steps to run the Job:

  • Login to CIS and navigate to identity provision

Source system à look for the source system which is created to fetch the user/groups from Ariba

 Click on job logs in IPS to check the status:

 Resolution:  By default the value configured for parameter (ariba.applications.group.members.page.size,ariba.applications.user.groups.page.size )  is 50, update it according to your need. If this doesn’t work, log a support ticket with SAP to increase the API rate limit.

Joule Icon Is Missing in Ariba despite completing all the configurations (running boosters, system added successfully in formations, SSO is enabled)

Resolution: Log a ticket with SAP to enable the feature PLUI 2928  at parent and child level

If you are facing any other issues, I would suggest to log a case with support team. To save time, make sure to share the logs and X-Correlation ID with support team. 

How to download the Joule Logs:

  • Login to Ariba application
  • Click on joule icon, reproduce the issue
  • Click on three bars --> settings  --> abouts --> download trances --> include message history --> download 

How to Get X Correlation ID?

  • Login to Ariba system
  • Enable logs:
    • Right-click on browser, select "Inspect"
    • once the Developer Tools are open, locate and click on the "Network" tab
  • Open Joule (keep the Developer Tools open)
  • Reproduce the issue you are experiencing
  • When the issue is reproduced:
    • in the Network tab, identify the most recent API call to Joule. This API call will be named with a UUID (for example: c1234b04-c313-42cd-9be3-a5efe9b0f2d1).
    • click on the API request and go to the "Headers" section;
    • scroll down to find and collect the following fields:
      • X-correlationid
      • Timestamp,
      • JouleDataCenter (you can find this in the "API Request URL")

Ariba-Joule support queues: you may choose the queue based on the nature of the error. 

✨Conclusion
The most common Ariba–Joule issues often stem from small but critical configuration gaps across Ariba, IAS, IPS, and Build Work Zone—and fixing these resolves the majority of navigation, transactional, and sync failures.
With the right configurations in place, Joule delivers the seamless, intelligent experience it’s designed for—helping customers unlock real value without post‑go‑live roadblocks. 🚀

Hello SAP Ariba Supplier Management & Risk (SM&R) Community!

If you're interested in learning about some of the new features coming with our May release, you're in the right place. 

Let's take a look at what's new within SM&R this quarter...

 

SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance

Additional Authorizations for AI Copilot Joule Scenarios in Supplier Management (SLP-2412)

This feature refines the requirements for user group membership to see prompts for specific Joule supplier management scenarios. This refinement ensures that prompts related to specific aspects of supplier management functionality are only visible  to users with relevant permissions, in customer landscapes that include the applicable solutions.

 

 

 

Ability to Restrict the Number of Commodity, Region, and Department Answers in External Questionnaires (SLP-2382)

This feature enables you to configure the maximum number of answers process initiators can add to Commodity, Region and Department questions in the external modular questionnaire.

Process initiators can only add the maximum number of answers you specify when creating a process, ensuring that processes meet your business requirements. It is applicable for external modular questionnaire. If the data is pre-populated from the registration stage or initial values specified from the template, the selected items need to be within the defined levels in the template configuration. If the pre-populated answers exceed the specified range, you must remove the values that are outside of the defined levels in the template configuration. 

 

 

SAP Ariba Supplier Risk

Additional Joule Capabilities in SAP Ariba Supplier Risk (SRISK-1860)

Your AI copilot Joule integrates with the Risk Exposure API - making it that much faster to find information via natural language prompting.

Take a look at these examples: 

 

Enhanced Virus scanning capability in Supplier Risk (SRISK-1329)

This feature automatically scans all files uploaded during different stages of an engagement request for viruses and malware, providing enhanced security protection throughout the supplier onboarding process. When documents are uploaded during any stage of creating an engagement request, each file is scanned in real-time before the next upload can begin. This sequential upload process ensures thorough security screening of documents.

Previously, you could upload multiple files consecutively without interruption. The system now requires a scan to complete before you can upload the next file. Please allow a brief moment between file uploads.

 

 

 

Enhancing Risk Exposure API by Adding Standard and Custom Category in Response (SRISK-1856)

 This feature enables the Risk Exposure API to retrieve responses for both standard and custom risk categories for suppliers you monitor in SAP Ariba Supplier Risk. The responses depend on the parameter setting for Enable custom risk categories (Application.SR.Risk.EnableCustomRiskCategories) on your site.

The current version (v3) of Risk Exposure API returns responses regardless of the parameter setting. 

When the Enable custom risk categories parameter is enabled, the API returns data for your custom risk categories.

When the parameter is disabled, the API automatically returns data for the default risk categories: Environmental & Social, Financial, Operational, and Regulatory & Legal.

(The previous version (v2) of the Risk Exposure API returned responses only when the Enable custom risk categories parameter was enabled.)

entry.title: Your S/4HANA & Ariba implementation is live, but your GRC ruleset do not have Ariba rules configured
entry.content:
Most SAP GRC implementations have a blind spot.

It is called Ariba.

And if your SoD ruleset doesn't account for it, you may be signing off clean access reviews on a system that's wide open to procurement fraud.

Across numerous SAP GRC implementations and Pre Go-Live and Post Go-Live reviews across the region, I typically get one of three responses when I ask whether the SoD ruleset covers cross-application risks between S/4HANA and Ariba:

  • "SAP GRC doesn't support integration with Ariba."
  • "We don't have IAG (Identity Access Governance)."
  • "We are planning to do it as part of Phase 2."

Let me translate those for you:

  • means "we haven't figured it out yet"
  • means "we know it's a gap but haven't prioritised it yet"
  • means "we are hoping the auditors don't notice before Phase 2"

That’s not a configuration gap. That’s your next audit finding !!!

The Integration Gap

1. GRC has no native Ariba connector.

Unlike the standard S/4HANA connector that pulls user assignments, role assignments, and authorisation objects, Ariba is opaque to GRC. There's no out-of-the-box integration. 

2. Ariba doesn't expose authorisations the way S/4HANA does.

There is no PFCG equivalent where you can drill into what a user can actually do in Ariba. No authorisation objects. No field-level permissions. Just system groups with pre-defined permissions.

3. In practice, this means a user could be registering fictitious suppliers in Ariba and processing invoices in S/4HANA and your GRC system would see nothing wrong.

So What Can You Do?

Here's the practical workaround I have implemented across multiple clients. The workaround is elegant in its simplicity where we bring Ariba into GRC's language by representing Ariba groups as custom Tcodes and template roles in S/4HANA.

To gain a better understanding of the SAP Ariba authorisation design, please review the list of access groups available in Ariba using the link below.

https://help.sap.com/docs/strategic-sourcing/strategic-sourcing-and-supplier-management-group-descriptions/strategic-sourcing-and-supplier-management-group-descriptions

SAP Ariba uses a group-based authorisation model where access is determined entirely by group membership.

Standard groups delivered in Ariba have fixed, pre-defined permissions that cannot be modified. While customers can create custom groups, these are essentially collections of standard groups (through group nesting) and do not allow individual permissions or actions to be customised, unlike PFCG roles.

Unlike PFCG roles, you cannot hand-pick permissions across Ariba groups. The permission boundary is always the standard groups and custom groups are simply collections of those standard groups.

For cross-application SoD analysis, the assessment should be performed between the user's assigned Ariba groups and their S/4HANA roles/access. As Ariba access is governed by group membership, the effective permissions granted by the Ariba groups should be evaluated together with the user's S/4HANA access to identify potential SoD conflicts.

Example

This is a standard SAP Ariba system group. If I want to create a custom group called "Supplier Onboarding Team Member (SUPP_ONB_TEAM_MEM)", I would create the custom group and assign the relevant system group as its parent group. The custom group would then inherit the permissions from that system group.

The Solution

Step 1: Create Custom Tcodes for Ariba System Groups. A sample is shown in the below screenshot. The Tcode descriptions can be written in simple, business-friendly language so that end users can easily understand the purpose of each group without requiring technical knowledge.

Step 2: Create template or dummy roles for ARIBA groups in S4HANA. Let us assume that you have an ARIBA group with name "Supplier Onboarding Team Member", you can create a PFCG role as per your own naming convention.

ARIBA GroupS/4HANA role nameDescription
Supplier Onboarding Team MemberAR:S_SUPPLIER_ONBOARDING_TEAMSee screenshot below

Maintain a comprehensive description of the role, including all actions that can be performed by users assigned to it in Ariba. This enables more effective access reviews, role design validation, and SoD risk assessments.

With the above approach, SAP Ariba groups are represented as template (dummy) roles in SAP S/4HANA, while Ariba system groups are represented as custom Tcodes in SAP S/4HANA.

Step 3:  This is the critical step. Without it, Steps 1 and 2 are just housekeeping. Mapping the Ariba Tcodes into your GRC ruleset is what transforms a workaround into a functioning control.  This will enable access risk analysis to identify potential Segregation of Duties (SoD) conflicts and critical access risks arising from Ariba groups. The custom Ariba Tcodes should be mapped to existing business functions and risk definitions within the Ruleset. New functions and risks may also be created to address Ariba-specific activities.

This approach ensures that Ariba access assignments, whether provisioned directly or through composite roles, are included in access risk analysis and remain subject to the client's governance, risk, and compliance controls.

Here is a real SoD risk that spans both systems and would be completely missed without this approach. Maintain a fictitious vendor and enter a Vendor invoice for automatic payment

  • Vendor Master Maintenance (ZPR01) + Process Vendor Invoices (ZAP02)

I have included the ARIBA Tcodes related to the supplier maintenance in this Vendor Master Maintenance function.

When a user who has access to process vendor invoices is being granted with the Supplier Onboarding Team Member (Ref S4HANA Role: AR:S_SUPPLIER_ONBOARDING_TEAM) group in ARIBA, the corresponding SOD risks will be highlighted as shown in the below screenshot.

The SoD risk didn't exist in S/4HANA alone. It didn't exist in Ariba alone. It existed in the combination of access across both systems and was  invisible to  GRC ruleset, invisible to most access reviews, and invisible to auditors who don't know to look for it.

That's the gap this approach closes.

Your GRC ruleset should reflect the reality of how your users actually work across applications and not within silos. If Ariba is part of your procurement landscape and those functions are not in your ruleset, your SoD analysis is not complete.

Don't let your blind spot become your audit finding.

Extending the GRC Ruleset — What Else Can You Define?

The supplier onboarding example above is just one of many cross-system SoD conflicts that become visible once Ariba is brought into your GRC ruleset.

Using the same custom Tcodes approach, you can define risks across the full procurement lifecycle. Here are some examples:

ARIBA AccessS/4HANA AccessPotential Risk Scenario
Register / onboard suppliersExecute payment runFictitious vendor fraud
Electronically sign contractsProcess vendor invoicesContract approval + Invoice processing by same person
Create sourcing projects & requisitionsPost goods receiptsFull P2P cycle without segregation
Mass update contractsMaintain purchase ordersBulk reprice contracts then self-raise POs

The pattern is consistent i.e., the fraud doesn't live in one system. It lives in the combination.

Once your Ariba groups are represented as custom Tcodes in GRC, any of these risks can be configured, monitored and reported just like any native S/4HANA SoD conflict.

Thank you for reading. I hope this gives you a practical starting point for bridging the Ariba–S/4HANA SoD coverage gap in your GRC implementation.

If you have questions, have implemented something similar, or want to share your own approach, please drop a comment below.

You can also reach me directly at Maddysmail26@gmail.com whether it's a quick question, a deeper implementation challenge, or just a conversation about SAP.

Let's continue learning, sharing and building on each other's experience 🙂

SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance

 

Email Status Trackers for Modular Questionnaire Invitations [SLP-2429]

You can use this group to restrict who can create and edit contacts more narrowly than the default permissions, allowing for better governance of contact management.

 

Email Status Trackers for Modular Questionnaire Invitations [SLP-2399]

Risk mitigation.

 

 

SAP Ariba Supplier Risk

 

Stronger Malware Protection for Supplier File Uploads [SRISK-1895]

Files uploaded to SAP Ariba Supplier Risk are now scanned with enhanced malware detection that identifies a broader range of threats. Any file flagged as malicious is automatically blocked before it can be stored or accessed. This keeps your procurement data secure and ensures only safe files enter your supplier risk workflows.

 

View group members directly in Engagement Request approval workflows [SRISK-1897]

Group names assigned to tasks in Engagement Request approval workflows are now clickable links. entry.title: A Supplier Failure Is Never Just a Supplier Problem
entry.content:
In the first article in this series, we explored how supplier data is fragmented across functions — how six different teams each hold a different view of the same supplier, and no single team has the complete picture. In the second, we looked at the hidden complexity of supplier ecosystems: sub-tier supply chains, network-level changes, and signals that exist across multiple systems but are visible to none of them individually. In this article, the question becomes more fundamental: why do those blind spots matter — and who bears the consequences when they go unmanaged?

A batch fails quality inspection. The hold is placed. The investigation begins. Planning, procurement, manufacturing and quality teams gather to determine the best path forward with minimum disruption. These conversations focus rightly on root cause, corrective action, alternate sourcing and production rescheduling.

What rarely appears in those conversations is - Patient.

  • Someone who has been waiting for a treatment.
  • Someone who may not know why the delay is happening or how long it will last.
  • Someone for whom additional waiting time is not just an inconvenience but could be a matter of life and death. 

Supplier quality management is not functionally owned only by procurement or quality teams. In life sciences, it is a strategic business continuity capability that directly impacts product availability, patient safety and organizational reputation. Supplier risk is not simply a supply chain issue. Ultimately, it is a patient safety issue.

The Invisible Connection Between Suppliers and Patients

Most organizations think of supplier management in terms of categories, contracts, performance scorecards and quality records. These are the right tools for managing operational supplier relationships. But they do not make visible the connection that runs from the supplier all the way to the patient.

That connection looks like this:

Supplier --> Raw Materials --> Manufacturing --> Product --> Supply Chain --> Distribution --> Patient 

What the supplier delivers — and the timeliness of that delivery directly determines whether the patient receives their treatment on time & at the right quality standard. 

A supplier quality failure does not stay at the supplier. It travels through every link in that chain. And in life sciences, where products are often critical therapies with no readily available substitutes, the consequences of supply disruption can extend far beyond a production delay.

Why Supplier Risk Is Consistently Underestimated

Traditionally, suppliers are evaluated on quality scorecards, audit results and delivery performance — all based on historical transactions. These are valuable indicators, but they are backward-looking by design. Supplier intelligence requires a different orientation: not 'how did this supplier perform last quarter?' but 'what signals exist today that indicate a risk in the coming weeks?'

Cost of Discovering Risk Too Late

Consider a clinical trial site ready to receive a scheduled delivery of investigational product kits. Patients have been enrolled, the investigator has confirmed site readiness and the planning team has confirmed kit availability. Three days before the delivery window, the approved logistics partner reports a capacity issue. The kit supplier, trying to protect the timeline, arranges an alternative carrier without notifying the sponsor. The replacement carrier is not GDP-qualified and is not listed in the IMP dossier as an approved distribution partner.

The kits arrive on schedule. The site accepts the delivery. The issue surfaces only weeks later, during a routine audit. By that point, the question of trial integrity is already on the table and the regulatory response cannot be avoided. The investigation is necessary, the corrective action is expensive and the trial timeline is affected. But the most significant loss is not the cost of the regulatory finding. It is the loss of the opportunity to prevent it — because the supplier's decision was made without notification, and no process existed to detect the change before it reached the trial.

The Role of Supplier Intelligence in Protecting Patients

The gap is not in the availability of supplier data. Most organizations hold significant information about their suppliers — qualification records, audit findings, delivery performance, change notifications. The gap is in the absence of a capability that connects those signals across functions, recognises change patterns early and surfaces them to the people who can act — before the event reaches the product, the trial or the patient.

The difference between a supplier performance management system and a supplier intelligence system is not the quantity of data it holds. It is the quality of the questions it can answer: not 'how did this supplier perform last quarter?' but 'what is this supplier likely to do in the next six weeks, and what should we do about it today?'

The Strategic Question

The question for life sciences leaders is not simply 'Are our suppliers compliant?' The more strategic question is: 'Can we use connected intelligence to make better supplier decisions — so that our patients continue to receive the treatment they need, on time, at the right quality, without interruption?'

To conclude, supplier quality in life sciences cannot be viewed as a standalone operational process. Every supplier decision is potentially connected to production planning, manufacturing resilience, product availability and patient trust. The supplier management process must evolve — not just to manage compliance, but to identify risks early, understand their potential impact across the value chain and provide recommendations for action before the patient is affected.

Next in this series (Article 4 of 6):  The Supplier Quality Platform That Thinks Ahead — From alerts and dashboards to AI-powered supplier intelligence.

entry.title: SAP Ariba Supplier Management & Risk 2611 Release Highlights
entry.content:
Hello SAP Ariba Supplier Management & Risk Community, 

Let's take a look at some of the features included in the Q4 2026 release for SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle & Performance and SAP Ariba Supplier Risk solutions. 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle & Performance

Dimension-Based Filters for Supplier Evaluations [NGSM-3344]

This feature offers expanded filtering capabilities across supplier evaluation screens to help you find relevant evaluations more efficiently. You can now filter results using dimensions such as Geographical Region, Product Classification, Company Code, and other available dimensions. These new filters are available on key evaluation pages, making it easier to narrow down participants, questionnaires, and evaluation programs based on the dimensions most relevant to your organization.


Supplier Performance Evaluations: Add Participants to Programs in In-Progress and No-Response Status [NGSM-3350]

You can now add internal participants to an evaluation program and assign suppliers to them while the program cycle is in In Progress or No Response status. Previously, participants could only be added during program creation, before the cycle started. With this enhancement, program owners and program creators can add new participants and assign suppliers to them directly from the program detail page, even after the evaluation cycle has begun. A record of each change—including the user who made it, the timestamp, and the details of the change—is logged and displayed in the application.


Action Plan Management Integration with Supplier Profile [NGSM-3467]

You can now access and manage action plans from multiple entry points in the SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance interface, including the Manage menu and the supplier profile.


Supplier Questionnaire: Flexible Mapping in Scorecard [NGSM-3471]

You can now assign different sets of suppliers to individual questionnaires within a single evaluation program. Previously, all suppliers had to be mapped to every questionnaire before the program could be submitted. With this enhancement, you can independently map any subset of suppliers to each questionnaire, enabling multi-region assessments within one program; for example, mapping region-specific suppliers to separate regional questionnaires. The program can be submitted as long as each questionnaire has at least one supplier assigned.


Ability to Update ERP Vendor IDs for Integrated Suppliers Using Data Import [SLP-2349]

This feature adds the ability to use the Suppliers data import task in SM Administration to update ERP vendor IDs for integrated supplies. Previously, it was only possible to update ERP vendor IDs for suppliers with Not Integrated or In Process integration status or suppliers whose initial synchronization to the ERP system was in an error state using this data import.


Support for Flex Master Data in Supplier Management Questionnaires [SLP-2413]

This feature adds the ability to questions based on custom flex master data in supplier management questionnaires. You can use existing flex master data features to create custom data structures for storing master data specific to your organization, then add questions related to that data to supplier requests or registration questionnaires. Questionnaire respondents choose from flex master data values when adding answers.


Support for Setting Modular Questionnaire Project-Level Status to Archived for Archived Risk Assessments [SLP-2430]

This feature adds support for setting the project-level status of modular questionnaires archived as part of an engagement risk assessment project where they're included as risk assessments to Archived status. Setting these projects to Archived status at the project level means that all of their data remains available, approval graphs are never reset, and a clear audit trail of project activity is maintained.


Ability to Mass Cancel In-Progress Supplier Registration Projects [SLP-2456]

This feature adds the ability to mass cancel supplier registration projects with a registration status of *Invited*, *In Registration*, *Pending Approval*, or *Pending Resubmit*. Administrators use a data import task to specify the suppliers with registration projects in these statuses to cancel in a single operation. Previously, it was only possible to cancel registration projects individually using a manual procedure.

 

SAP Ariba Supplier Risk

Ability to View and Navigate to the Associated Engagement Request from the Contract Workspace [SRISK-1891]

This feature enables you to navigate directly from a Contract Workspace to its associated Engagement Request (ER) in Supplier Risk through a clickable Engagement Request ID link. The link opens the ER at the exact page where it was last left, and Go back to contract banner allows you to return seamlessly to the originating contract. You can review and edit the ER as permitted, completing contract and risk reviews in one continuous workflow.


Ability to Export Engagement List Status in English Across All Locales [SRISK-1900]

This feature enables you to export the engagement list with the *Status* column including phase name and status label in English, regardless of the locale in which the engagement request was created or the user's locale.


Ability to Execute Bulk Template Upgrades for Selected Engagement Requests [SRISK-1908]

This feature enables you to upgrade multiple selected engagement requests to a newer template version in a single bulk operation, eliminating the need to upgrade each engagement individually. Template upgrade enables you to update existing control-based engagement risk assessment projects to the latest published version of the supplier risk engagement template, ensuring your engagements always reflect your organization's most recent risk processes.

entry.title: Finding Success During Implementation and Adoption
entry.content:
Finding Success During Implementation and Adoption

Lessons from Sumeet Kulshrestha on turning procurement technology into sustainable business value

💡A procurement transformation can reach go-live and still fall short of its promise. In this episode of The Future of Procurement Podcast, Sumeet Kulshrestha, VP, Delivery - Finance & Spend Management (FSM) at SAP, draws on more than two decades in procurement services to explain why implementation success depends on more than technology. His message is practical: organizations create value when they connect business ownership, governance, adoption, integrations, and continuous improvement from the start.

Go-live is the starting line, not the finish line

🚦One of the most important reframes in the discussion is that go-live should not be treated as the destination. The real transformation begins when people start using the system; transactions begin flowing, and the organization learns whether new processes work across procurement, finance, accounts payable, HR, and other connected functions. Sumeet notes that many challenges surface after deployment, which makes ongoing attention to adoption and value realization essential.

🌱That changes how leaders should think about implementation. A launch is not a one-time technology event. It is the start of a sustained operating model in which processes evolve, people change roles, organizations acquire businesses, and new capabilities become available. The companies that keep "watering the plant" are better positioned to continuously improve rather than freezing their transformation at the moment of go-live.

Fit to standard, then customize with purpose

🧭 Cloud solutions have changed the customization equation. In the on-premise era, organizations could modify core code so extensively that upgrades became difficult. Today, cloud platforms create stronger boundaries. That makes a fit-to-standard mindset valuable, but it does not mean every configuration or customization is harmful.

⚙️The sharper question is why a deviation is needed. Customizing technology simply to reproduce an old process can preserve complexity instead of removing it. But a targeted change that supports a meaningful business outcome can become a source of innovation. Sumeet points to invoicing against a contract as an example of a customer-created capability that ultimately informed broader product innovation. The test is whether the change is scalable, outcome-driven, and worth the long-term operational cost.

Procurement transformation is an enterprise transformation

🔗Procurement does not operate on an island. Sourcing, buying, contracting, invoicing, supplier processes, and external workforce activities connect to systems and teams across the enterprise. A procurement deployment that overlooks those dependencies can create friction elsewhere, even if the procurement design itself appears sound.

👥This is why business involvement matters so much. The strongest projects put knowledgeable stakeholders at the table early and give them enough capacity and authority to make decisions. Rather than asking IT to push a solution into the business, organizations need procurement, finance, AP, HR, IT, and other affected groups to shape how the new operating model will work together.

Governance turns debate into decisions

🛠️ Projects can also stall when ownership is unclear and every decision is pursued through consensus. Effective governance needs named decisionmakers, regular cadence, clear agenda items, and the authority to resolve trade-offs. Implementation partners add more value when they present genuinely distinct options and explain the consequences, rather than transferring a long menu of choices back to the customer.

🎯For adoption, Sumeet favors pragmatic rollout strategies over unnecessary big-bang risk. Start with receptive users or a manageable group, prove that the process works, learn from real behavior, and expand. In some cases, pairing enthusiastic users with demanding stakeholders can expose weaknesses early while still creating advocates for the change.

When something feels wrong, act early

🚨The most expensive solution is one an organization buys but does not use. If adoption is weak, value is not materializing, or the implementation feels off-course, waiting only compounds the problem. Sumeet recommends asking for help early and using an honest health assessment to understand where outcomes are being lost.

📈His recovery model is straightforward: assess, stabilize, and optimize. First, identify the root causes across technology, process, integration, governance, and adoption. Next, stabilize the operating environment and decision model. Then optimize the outcomes that justified the investment in the first place. Asking for help is not a sign of failure. It is evidence that leaders are serious about protecting the business case.

AI expands the toolkit, but people still matter

🤖AI will increasingly handle repeatable work and add new capabilities to procurement, but Sumeet does not see it eliminating the human dimension of transformation. Judgment, context, governance, and connection to customers remain central. In that sense, the familiar three-legged stool of people, process, and technology may gain another leg: AI, governed deliberately and used to extend what teams can accomplish.

✅The takeaway is simple: procurement transformations do not fail because they encounter speed bumps. They fail when organizations stop steering. Success comes from treating the implementation as an enterprise change, making decisions with discipline, staying close to users after go-live, and intervening early when value starts to drift.

Take the next step
